topic: Why volcanoes erupt: the parts of a volcano and what pushes the magma out
title: Why Volcanoes Erupt
subtitle: What pushes hot rock out
objectives: Name the main parts of a volcano
Tell the difference between magma and lava
Explain how gas bubbles and pressure push magma out
art_direction: flat vector illustration, soft shadows, warm friendly colors, clean rounded shapes, playful kid friendly

scenes.title: Shake it and it blows!
scenes.narration: Have you ever shaken a soda bottle. Whoosh. Foam shoots up. A volcano is a bit like that, but with super hot rock and gas bubbles.
scenes.image_prompt: a sunny kitchen table closeup with a plastic soda bottle fizzing over, white foam spraying up, two kid hands pulling back in surprise

narration.text: Have you ever shaken a soda bottle. Whoosh. Foam shoots up. A volcano is a bit like that, but with super hot rock and gas bubbles.

scenes.title: Hot rock hiding below
scenes.narration: In places with volcanoes, deep under the ground, heat melts rock. It makes a thick liquid called magma. It is trapped and squeezed, and it starts to rise.
scenes.image_prompt: glowing underground closeup of dark rock with cracks filled with bright orange melted rock, heat glow and small bubbles

narration.text: In places with volcanoes, deep under the ground, heat melts rock. It makes a thick liquid called magma. It is trapped and squeezed, and it starts to rise.

scenes.title: Parts of a Volcano
scenes.narration: The magma chamber at the bottom holds melted rock. The vent is the tunnel it climbs through. The crater is the bowl at the top. Outside, we call it lava.
scenes.image_prompt: cross section view of a volcano mountain with green slopes, glowing red melted rock pocket underground connected by a vertical tunnel to a bowl opening at the top, red flow on the side

narration.text: The magma chamber at the bottom holds melted rock. The vent is the tunnel it climbs through. The crater is the bowl at the top. Outside, we call it lava.

scenes.title: Bubbles push hard
scenes.narration: Gas bubbles grow in magma like bubbles in soda. They take up room, so pressure builds. Gassy magma can burst out. Runny magma with little gas oozes calmly.
scenes.manim_brief: Show a simple volcano cross section. Step 1: red magma sits in a round chamber. Step 2: small white gas bubbles appear in magma, grow bigger and rise fast into the vent, with arrows showing pressure building. Step 3: show two outcomes side by side: gassy thick magma bursts up out of crater, runny low-gas magma oozes gently out and flows as lava.

narration.text: Gas bubbles grow in magma like bubbles in soda. They take up room, so pressure builds. Gassy magma can burst out. Runny magma with little gas oozes calmly.

scenes.title: Quick check
scenes.narration: What pushes magma out of a volcano. Pause and pick your answer. Is it gas bubbles and pressure, cold rain, wind blowing, or the Moon pulling.
scenes.image_prompt: closeup inside a dark rock crack filled with glowing red magma and rising white gas bubbles growing bigger as they move up

quiz.question: What pushes magma out of a volcano?
quiz.explanation: Gas bubbles grow and build pressure that pushes magma up the vent.

narration.text: What pushes magma out of a volcano. Pause and pick your answer. Is it gas bubbles and pressure, cold rain, wind blowing, or the Moon pulling.

reveal.text: Gas bubbles and pressure. Gas bubbles grow and build pressure that pushes magma up the vent.

scenes.title: Volcanoes blow like soda
scenes.narration: Magma chamber stores melted rock. Vent carries it up. Gas pushes it out as lava, bursting or oozing. Where have you seen bubbles lift liquid. Next time: why does some lava flow calmly while other volcanoes explode sky-high.
scenes.image_prompt: friendly volcano with red lava flowing calmly down one side and a small puff bursting from the top, green landscape around

narration.text: Magma chamber stores melted rock. Vent carries it up. Gas pushes it out as lava, bursting or oozing. Where have you seen bubbles lift liquid. Next time: why does some lava flow calmly while other volcanoes explode sky-high.

checks.question: 1. Would someone stop? First 3 seconds with recognizable object
checks.reason: Opens with a spraying soda bottle and kid hands pulling back, a familiar surprising object not a logo or definition.

checks.question: 2. Would they want to start the lesson? Title clear without prior knowledge
checks.reason: Title Why Volcanoes Erupt uses plain kid-known words with the search word volcanoes first and under 40 characters.

checks.question: 3. Would someone watch to the end? New visual every 15s
checks.reason: Scenes 2, 5 and 6 have null image_prompt and null manim_brief, creating text-only stretches where attention will drop.
checks.fix: Add a visual for every gap: glowing underground magma close-up for scene 2, bubbling magma column animation for quiz, lava-flow recap image for summary, with no static shot over 3s.

checks.question: 4. Would they participate? Open question from experience
checks.reason: Ends with Where else have you seen bubbles push liquid up plus a pause-and-pick quiz, both answerable from everyday life.

checks.question: 5. Would they be satisfied? Hook promise fulfilled inside
checks.reason: Soda-bubble promise is answered inside by naming chamber, vent, crater, lava and showing bubbles building pressure.

checks.question: 6. Would they rewatch? Serves as reference
checks.reason: Timeless labeled volcano diagram and 3-line recap can be reused for study and to explain to another child.

checks.question: 7. Would they return? Concrete named reason to come back
checks.reason: Summary closes with recap and question but names no next video or topic to return for.
checks.fix: Add a named next-lesson hook in last line, e.g.: Next time: why does some lava flow calmly while other volcanoes explode sky-high?

fact_issues: Hook says 'A volcano works the same way' as shaken soda: overstates analogy; shaking does not trigger volcanoes and soda CO2 nucleation differs from magmatic volatiles, heat, viscosity and buoyancy.
Implies all eruptions end in 'boom' from bubbles: omits effusive eruptions where runny low-gas magma oozes without explosion.
Says magma is 'Deep below your feet' as if everywhere: magma chambers exist only under volcanic areas, not under all feet.

video_review.summary: Clear and age appropriate lesson on why volcanoes erupt. The soda and bubbles analogy, labeled diagrams and quiz work well for 5th grade. Small fixes to lava labeling, pacing of vocabulary, quiz time and the closing question would make it ready for class use.
strengths: Strong soda bottle analogy that matches the eruption idea for this age group.
Voice narration stays in sync with large on screen titles, labels and simple diagrams.
Word by word captions with highlighting support reading.
Quiz question directly checks the main idea and gives a clear correct answer with explanation.
Short recap of chamber, vent and gas bubbles reinforces vocabulary.

notes.issue: At about 0:33 the voice says Outside we call it lava, but the volcano picture has no lava tag. Only the word list on the right shows lava, so students cannot see where lava is.
notes.fix: Add a visible lava label with an arrow pointing to the red flow on the side of the volcano and keep it on screen while the narration says the word lava.

notes.issue: At about 0:26 four new terms magma chamber, vent, crater and lava are introduced within about ten seconds, which is too fast for many 10 to 11 year olds to remember.
notes.fix: Add a short pause between terms and show the full labeled volcano again for three to four seconds so students can review all four words together.

notes.issue: At about 1:00 the quiz timer counts down from 8 seconds, which is short for slower readers to read four choices and decide.
notes.fix: Extend the think time to at least 12 seconds and add a clear on screen prompt that says Pause now for teachers.

notes.issue: At about 1:24 the closing asks two questions at once and the second one about why some lava flows calmly while others explode sky high introduces a new topic that is not explained.
notes.fix: Keep one closing question such as Where have you seen bubbles push liquid up, and save calm versus explosive eruptions for the next lesson.
